headline: High-risk default workspace overlap: Claude Code can write and modify git state while the prompt-list agent is unisolated and may be consumed as instructions, creating leakage and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a prompt/content-writing source with docs-only evidence and no isolation; agent B reads files, uses stdin/stdout, and can use MCP, so A’s content can be fed into B as trusted instructions. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven, but the file-based bridge is plausible.
conditions: IF agent A content is copied into files or stdin consumed by agent B, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF agent B parses A-produced text as instructions without provenance checks, malicious prompt content can steer actions.
mitigations: Keep A outputs in a separate review-only folder.
Require a human to strip instructions before B ingests A content.
Disable MCP inputs for any A-derived text.
Add a provenance header marking A content as untrusted.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or allowlist parsing before B consumes external text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B has broad network egress, filesystem read/write, and handles repo files and cwd contents; agent A is docs-only and may produce content that is later stored in shared files. The pair does not show PHI or secrets, so this is leakage of workspace content rather than confirmed sensitive data, but the shared filesystem path makes it plausible in default use.
conditions: IF A-derived files are placed in the same cwd as B, B can read them.
IF B forwards workspace contents to external APIs or MCP servers, those contents can leave the host.
mitigations: Store A outputs outside B’s working directory.
Review B’s outbound destinations before running it.
Remove secrets from any shared folder.
Use separate OS users or directories for the two agents.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation or egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write the filesystem and modify git state, and its concurrency model says shared state with other instances is via filesystem and git only. Agent A has no write controls, but if its outputs are materialized into the same repo, B can overwrite or race on those files. The default shared mutable surface makes conflict likely and potentially destructive.
conditions: IF A-generated files are committed into the same repository B edits, git conflicts can occur.
IF multiple B instances run on the same workspace, filesystem races are possible.
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate clone.
Pause one agent before the other edits shared files.
Use git branches per agent.
Check for uncommitted changes before starting B.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared workspace and git operations.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A produces prompt collections/content, and agent B can act on file and shell inputs with broad permissions. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or malicious instructions can cascade into edits, installs, or shell actions. The pair lacks a built-in verification step, so the pathway exists in common workflows.
conditions: IF B uses A output as task instructions without verification, incorrect actions can propagate.
IF A output contains fabricated steps or commands, B may execute them through shell or git tools.
mitigations: Require B to summarize and confirm A’s instructions before acting.
Use a second human review for commands from A.
Block direct execution of A-authored shell snippets.
Keep A as reference-only, not task-authoritative.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before shell/git actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles git credentials and Anthropic API keys, while agent A is a public prompt-list source with no sensitive-data fields. There is no documented residency or certification mismatch between them, so the main issue is limited to handling secrets in B’s environment, not a pairwise compliance breach.
conditions: IF B is run in an environment containing regulated secrets, its handling of those secrets becomes relevant.
IF A-derived content is mixed with secret-bearing files, retention and logging policies may diverge.
mitigations: Do not place secrets in B’s workspace.
Rotate exposed credentials after testing.
Review logging settings for secret redaction.
Keep A content in a non-sensitive project.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls for secret-bearing workspaces.
